summary: Describes the use and detailed design of route servers that distribute routing information among BGP and IDRP routers, as an alternative to a full mesh of connections. It was experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of everyone phoning everyone else, all call one office that passes along the news.

questions: what is a bgp route server
how to avoid a full mesh of bgp peers
subtitle: Simplifying BGP and IDRP network routing using dedicated route servers instead of direct peering.

tldr.problem: Large networks using BGP or IDRP routing protocols require border routers to maintain direct connections with every other border router (full mesh), creating many connections to maintain. In switched networks like ATM, this becomes impractical.
tldr.mechanism: Route servers act as central hubs that collect routing information from border routers and distribute it to client routers. Clients connect only to their assigned route servers, not to each other. Route servers relay routes unmodified, so clients receive the same information as if directly peered.
tldr.outcome: This approach reduces connection complexity while preserving full routing information. Route servers can be clustered for redundancy. The RFC is Experimental and is now Historic, having influenced but not been widely adopted compared to direct BGP peering.

today: This RFC is Historic. Route servers were an experimental approach to reducing BGP complexity, but other techniques (such as route reflectors and confederations) became more widely adopted for scaling BGP deployments.

sections.title: The Full Mesh Problem
sections.content:
Border routers that participate in inter-domain routing using BGP-4 or IDRP must establish direct connections with every other border router in their domain to exchange external routing information. This creates an n-squared scaling problem: in a domain with 10 border routers, each router must maintain 9 connections, for a total of 45 peer connections across the domain.

In switched networks using ATM, SMDS, or Frame Relay, where many routers connect to a shared fabric, a full mesh becomes impractical. Adding a new border router means creating many new connections. This RFC proposes route servers to eliminate the full mesh requirement: border routers become clients that connect only to their assigned route server, not to each other. The route server relays all routing information unmodified, preserving the information clients need to make correct routing decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: With many routers, having every one talk to every other takes too many phone lines. A route server is like a central switchboard: each router just calls it, and it passes the messages along.

sections.title: Route Server Architecture
sections.content:
A route server is a process that collects routing information from border routers and distributes it to client routers. The key design principle is that route servers do NOT apply selection criteria to routes: all routes received are relayed unmodified (with their BGP or IDRP path attributes) to all clients.

Route servers can be either intra-domain (relaying external routes between routers in the same domain) or inter-domain (relaying routes between domains). One or more route servers form an RS Cluster for redundancy: all client routers connect to every route server in their assigned cluster. This ensures clients receive routing information even if one server fails.

The model uses two approaches for inter-cluster communication. In the full-mesh model, each route server maintains connections to every route server in other clusters. In the hierarchical model, route servers form a tree structure, with each server connecting only to designated other servers. Hierarchical topology is simpler but requires careful management to prevent routing loops using the RCID_PATH attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: One or more route servers sit between client routers, receiving and passing along their routing info without changing it. For safety, there can be multiple servers (a cluster) so if one fails, the others keep working.

sections.title: Client and Server Operation
sections.content:
A route server client (an RC) is any router that peers with a route server to acquire routing information. The client maintains a BGP or IDRP connection to every route server in its assigned cluster. Clients must recognize the ADVERTISER path attribute, a new optional attribute (type code 255) that identifies which border router originally submitted each route. Routes received from route servers are processed as if they came directly from the advertiser.

Route servers maintain standard BGP/IDRP sessions with clients, with one key difference: they include the ADVERTISER attribute in all UPDATE messages to show the original source. A route server accepts routes from its client border routers and from other route servers, then advertises them to all other clients. Routes received from one client are not echoed back to that client.

When route servers in the same cluster receive routes, they treat each other as if they were clients: identical routes from different servers in the cluster cause the old route to be replaced without triggering route advertisements. This minimizes duplicate routing updates. The RCID_PATH attribute (type code 254), used in hierarchical topologies, records the sequence of route server clusters a route has passed through, allowing detection of routing loops by checking for duplicate cluster IDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients tell the server 'I can reach this network', and the server says 'OK, I'll tell your neighbors.' Each message says who originally found the route, so everyone knows who to credit.

sections.title: Intra-Cluster Coordination
sections.content:
Route servers within the same cluster coordinate their activities to avoid redundant advertisements to clients. When two route servers share the same set of clients, ideally only one sends routing updates to each client. If a route server fails, the others take over its responsibility.

Route servers use LIST messages to tell each other which clients they are serving. Each server maintains an 'informed client' list for every server in its cluster and keeps them sorted by the number of clients served. When a server acquires a new client connection, it uses a delayed decision process: the server with the fewest clients gets to serve it first, determined by a delay timer based on its position in the sorted list. This load-balancing technique minimizes races and distributes clients evenly.

Route servers start in an Initiation state upon startup, during which they establish connections with other servers but do not yet send routing updates. Upon expiration of an InitiationTimer (suggested as 5 minutes) or when all configured connections are established, they transition to Active state and begin sending routing updates. If a route server loses a connection to another server in its cluster, it must assume responsibility for serving that failed server's clients (after checking they are not already served by another active server).
sections.plainLanguage: Multiple route servers in a group talk to each other to decide 'you take these clients, I'll take those.' If one goes down, the others split up its workload so nothing gets dropped.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
This RFC is Experimental and does not specify an Internet Standard. It was published in October 1995 and is now Historic. The approach described here influenced the design of routing infrastructures but was not widely adopted in favor of other techniques for scaling BGP deployments, such as route reflectors.

The document notes that this approach reduces the number of direct connections each border router must maintain but does NOT reduce the volume of routing information each router must process. It also does not propose any mechanism for dynamic discovery of route servers; routers must be manually configured with the address of their assigned route server or servers.
sections.plainLanguage: This was an experimental idea published in the 1990s. It helped people think about routing network design, but the industry ended up using different approaches. It's saved here for historical reference.
